analysis.one_liner: Delays any endangered-species protection for the greater sage grouse for a decade and lets governors override federal land plans.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, it never received a hearing or a vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from making any decision on listing the greater sage grouse under the Endangered Species Act until September 30, 2026, in any state with its own grouse management plan, and would have declared the bird's status 'not warranted' in the meantime [S2][S3]. It would also have stopped federal land agencies from amending their land-use plans for grouse habitat in ways a governor considered inconsistent with a state plan, for at least five years, and would have rolled back amendments made in the prior three years [S2][S3]. The governor of the state would get the final word on any disagreement, and the whole scheme would be exempt from court review [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and individuals that use or develop sagebrush federal lands — oil and gas drillers, hardrock and phosphate miners, and livestock operators with federal grazing permits — would benefit from a decade-long guarantee that the grouse cannot be listed, plus governor control over federal habitat plans in their states.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy, mining, and grazing interests on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Secretary of the Interior from making any Endangered Species Act listing finding on the greater sage grouse in states with state management plans before September 30, 2026, and declares the bird's conservation status 'not warranted' in the meantime [S2][S3].

Prohibits Interior and Agriculture from making withdrawals or amending federal resource management plans for grouse habitat in a way a governor says is inconsistent with the state plan, for at least five years after the governor's notification [S2][S3].

Retroactively stays federal plan amendments and withdrawals made in the three years before a governor's notification, restoring the earlier, less protective plan where they conflicted with the state plan [S3].
Gives the governor of the affected state final authority to resolve any disagreement over whether a federal action conflicts with the state plan [S3].
Exempts the entire scheme from judicial review, and provides that environmental findings under the National Environmental Policy Act cannot block federal actions consistent with a state plan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the sage grouse and the public's federal sagebrush lands would bear the cost: the Endangered Species Act backstop would be switched off for a decade no matter what the bird's numbers showed, federal agencies would lose their ability to adjust habitat protections, and courts could not hear challenges. The general public — hunters, wildlife watchers, and taxpayers with a stake in healthy public ranges — would share that risk, including the risk of a steeper decline later requiring more drastic and costly measures.
analysis.who_pays_short: The grouse, federal land agencies, and public-land users

drawbacks.text: The bill locks in a 'not warranted' listing status until 2026 'without regard to any other statute, regulation, court order, legal settlement,' removing the Endangered Species Act safety net even if sage grouse populations collapse in the meantime [S3].

It makes the governor of each state the final judge of whether federal habitat protections conflict with that state's plan — the same governor whose state plan the bill elevates — and then bars courts from reviewing that decision [S3].
It reaches backward, staying federal plan amendments adopted in the previous three years, undoing conservation measures that were already in effect [S3].

It provides that NEPA findings on grouse habitat 'shall not have a preclusive effect' on approving federal projects in states with state plans, weakening the standard environmental review of projects on public lands [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: By 2015 the Fish and Wildlife Service had found listing not warranted, largely because federal land-use plan amendments and state plans were put in place to protect grouse habitat — so some state-federal coordination was already working, and a case can be made for trusting state management. But this bill went well beyond coordination: it handcuffed federal agencies for a decade, let a governor overrule and even unwind federal conservation plans, appointed that same governor as judge of disputes, and shut off court review entirely. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill removed every check — legal, federal, and judicial — on whether state plans actually worked.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Rob Bishop of Utah introduced the bill on March 15, 2016, with 14 original cosponsors, all Republicans [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S5].
The 20 cosponsors it eventually drew were all Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken on the bill before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the existing arrangement stood: the 2015 federal land-use plan amendments for grouse habitat remained in force, the bird kept its 'not warranted' status subject to ongoing review, and federal agencies and courts kept their authority. The energy, mining, and grazing interests the bill was written for did not get their decade-long shield, and the species kept its legal protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sage grouse protections and federal land managers

for.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 original Republican cosponsors on the day of introduction

for.name: 20 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all 20 from the Republican side

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Republican — the sponsor and all 20 cosponsors — with no Democratic support recorded, but the bill never reached a vote, so the House's partisan split on it was never tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers on federal public lands
industries.note: Federal grouse habitat plans restrict drilling in the bird's core sagebrush range; a ten-year listing ban plus governor veto power over federal plan amendments would have eased those restrictions [S3]. The industry's gain would come at the cost of habitat protections the public owns the land for.

industries.industry: Hardrock and phosphate mining on federal land
industries.note: Mining on federal sagebrush acreage faces restrictions under grouse habitat plans; the bill would have blocked or rolled back plan amendments affecting grouse habitat for at least five years, with the governor deciding conflicts [S3].

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers holding federal grazing permits
industries.note: Federal grouse plan amendments limit grazing in key habitat; the bill's five-year freeze on amendments, its retroactive stay on the prior three years of amendments, and its bar on listing would have reduced pressure on grazing operations [S3].

industries.industry: Wildlife recreation and grouse hunting economy
industries.note: Ranchers, outfitters, and communities that rely on a healthy sage grouse population would bear the risk of a decade with no Endangered Species Act backstop and no court review, even if state plans failed.
